summary: Peer-to-peer applications create much of the traffic on the Internet. Traditional caches can reduce transit traffic but are complex to support for each application. This informational RFC states the problem DECADE addresses: in-network storage that applications can share.

plainLanguage.summary: Many people share files like trading cards. This memo asks whether the network could offer a shared locker so everyone does not travel far.

questions: how can p2p applications use in-network storage
how can in-network storage reduce p2p traffic
why are p2p caches complex to build
how would in-network storage differ from p2p caches
subtitle: In-network storage for P2P applications to reduce network stress.

tldr.problem: P2P applications like file sharing generate massive traffic that strains ISP networks, particularly on upload links. Traditional P2P caches can reduce traffic but are complex to build and do not give applications control over storage policies.
tldr.mechanism: DECADE proposes a standard protocol for P2P applications to store and retrieve data directly in in-network storage, with explicit policy controls. This decouples data access from the application's own signaling protocol.
tldr.outcome: A decoupled in-network storage service would let P2P applications manage bandwidth more efficiently and reduce uplink congestion, but no such standard protocol was widely adopted following this problem statement.

today: RFC 6646 is Informational and describes an unsolved problem. No widely adopted standard protocol for in-network storage emerged from this problem statement, though interest in content-centric networking and edge caching continues.

sections.title: P2P Traffic and Network Stress
sections.content:
Peer-to-peer applications, including file sharing and streaming, account for a large portion of Internet traffic in many networks, often reaching 50 to 90 percent of uplink traffic. A key inefficiency is that when a peer uploads a block of data to multiple other peers, that block traverses the peer's last-mile uplink once for each recipient. This concentrated uplink usage stresses ISP infrastructure and degrades performance, especially during peak demand such as flash crowds.

One way to reduce this stress is to introduce in-network storage: a service inside the network that holds data for P2P applications. A peer could upload once to in-network storage and many others could download from there, bypassing the peer's uplink entirely.
sections.plainLanguage: When you mail the same letter to ten friends, you have to drop it in the mailbox ten times. A better idea: drop it in a central mailbox and tell your friends to pick it up from there.

sections.title: In-Network Storage versus P2P Caches
sections.content:
In-network storage already exists, but mainly as application-specific P2P caches that understand the signaling and protocols of individual P2P applications. A P2P cache for BitTorrent must speak BitTorrent's protocol; a cache for another application must speak its protocol. This creates three problems for cache vendors. First, there are many P2P applications on the Internet, making it costly to support them all. Second, P2P applications evolve continuously, forcing vendors to track updates. Third, many applications use proprietary or encrypted protocols, making caches ineffective.

Without explicit control, a P2P cache may also increase download traffic if an end host has better connectivity to the cache than to remote peers.

DECADE proposes a different approach: a standard protocol that all applications can use to store and retrieve data in-network, without the cache needing to understand the application's proprietary protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now, a library needs to understand every type of book (comic books are shelved differently from textbooks). A better idea: give all books a simple label system that any library can use.

sections.title: BitTorrent and Content Publisher Scenarios
sections.content:
In a BitTorrent scenario, a client A normally uploads a block to many peers, consuming uplink capacity with each transfer. With in-network storage, client A uploads the block once to the storage, and other peers retrieve it from there. If the storage allows it, peer B can even upload to the storage while downloading, so the block is ready for peer C to download directly from storage.

Content publishers using hybrid CDN/P2P delivery also benefit. A publisher might distribute content via a CDN to a server, then allow P2P peers to distribute it further. In-network storage could buffer content at the network edge, reducing the need for every peer to upload over the last-mile link and allowing the publisher to control which content goes where.
sections.plainLanguage: A store puts popular items in a warehouse near the door, so shoppers do not have to go to the back room every time someone buys one.

sections.title: What In-Network Storage Needs to Provide
sections.content:
For in-network storage to work well, applications need basic mechanisms and flexibility to implement their own resource allocation policies. P2P applications have complex algorithms to select which peers are reliable sources and which are good recipients; they need to be able to keep refining these algorithms. A standard in-network storage protocol must allow applications to store content on demand, retrieve it, and set resource and access control policies (bandwidth limits, who can read and write, retention time).

The RFC notes that signaling and data access in P2P applications are distinct functions that are often coupled together in application protocols. By decoupling them, a standard data-access protocol becomes feasible: all applications could use the same wire protocol for storing and retrieving data, while keeping their own proprietary signaling protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: A good warehouse system lets each store owner decide how long to keep items and who can access them, rather than the warehouse telling the store what it can do.

sections.title: Security and Policy Risks
sections.content:
In-network storage raises several security and policy concerns. Attackers could try to consume storage space or exhaust connections via denial-of-service. Copyright and local laws may restrict what content can be stored or retrieved in certain regions, requiring filters or DRM. Eavesdropping on access messages is a risk, as is modification or replay of messages by a compromised middlebox. A malicious service provider could analyze what content users access to perform phishing attacks. Finally, unauthorized hosts could masquerade as legitimate clients to access protected storage.

The RFC identifies these threats but does not propose solutions; these are left to the protocol specification that would follow this problem statement.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared locker needs locks to keep thieves out, but also rules about what can be stored (no fireworks in some places), and care to keep secrets private.
